title: Find the first non-repeating character in a string (use a LinkedHashMap to count frequency, then find first with count 1).
shortTitle: Find the first non-repeating character in a string

s1_definition.profdef: The first non-repeating character is the earliest character in the string that appears exactly once. The standard solution makes two passes with a `LinkedHashMap`: the first pass counts the frequency of each character, and because LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, the second pass finds the first entry whose count is one. It is O(n) time and O(k) space where k is the number of distinct characters.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India generates coupon codes and needs to pick the first unique letter as a sub-key. In "SAVER" every letter is unique, so "S" wins, but in "SETTLES" the letter that appears only once and comes first is the answer. A clerk tallies every letter, then reads the code again from the start and picks the first letter whose tally is exactly one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count every character's frequency, then scan in original order and return the first one with a count of exactly one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The first non-repeating character is the earliest character in the string that appears exactly once. The standard solution makes two passes with a `LinkedHashMap`: the first pass counts the frequency of each character, and because LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, the second pass finds the first entry whose count is one. It is O(n) time and O(k) space where k is the number of distinct characters.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India generates coupon codes and needs to pick the first unique letter as a sub-key. In "SAVER" every letter is unique, so "S" wins, but in "SETTLES" the letter that appears only once and comes first is the answer. A clerk tallies every letter, then reads the code again from the start and picks the first letter whose tally is exactly one.

**One line to remember:** Count every character's frequency, then scan in original order and return the first one with a count of exactly one.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason a `LinkedHashMap` is chosen over a plain `HashMap` is ordering. A plain HashMap does not remember the order in which keys were inserted, so you could not reliably find the first unique character from the map alone. A LinkedHashMap keeps keys in insertion order, so iterating it yields characters in the order they first appeared, which is exactly what first means here.

The first pass iterates the string and does `freq.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum)`, which inserts the character with count 1 the first time and adds 1 on later appearances. The second pass iterates the LinkedHashMap's entries in insertion order and returns the key of the first entry whose value is 1. If no entry has a count of 1, there is no non-repeating character, and you return a sentinel such as a special value or an Optional.

An alternative second pass is to iterate the original string again and look up each character's count in the map, returning the first whose count is 1; this works with a plain HashMap too, because the string itself provides the order. Both are O(n) time. The LinkedHashMap approach is elegant because the order lives in the map. Space is O(k) for the distinct characters, bounded by the alphabet size.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India generates promotional coupon codes for Rajesh and needs to derive a sub-key from the first letter that appears only once in the code, to reduce collisions. The system must find the first non-repeating character. This is exactly how the first-unique algorithm works — count then scan.

Problem 2 — Some codes have no unique letter at all, like "AABB", and the system must handle that gracefully instead of crashing. This is exactly why we return a clear sentinel when no character has a count of one.

The code has a `CouponKeyService` class with a `firstUnique` method using a LinkedHashMap. The demo processes several codes.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: code `"SETTLES"`.

Step 1 — Pass one counts characters into the LinkedHashMap in insertion order: S appears at positions 0 and 6 so S is 2, E appears at 1 and 5 so E is 2, T appears at 2 and 3 so T is 2, L appears once so L is 1. The map order is S, E, T, L.

Step 2 — Pass two iterates the map in that order. S has count 2, skip. E has count 2, skip. T has count 2, skip. L has count 1, so return L.

Step 3 — For `"SAVER"` every character is unique, so the first entry S has count 1 and is returned. For `"AABB"` both A and B have count 2, so no entry has count 1 and the method returns null, logged as NONE.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Code 'SETTLES' first unique char = L
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Code 'SAVER' first unique char = S
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Code 'AABB' first unique char = NONE
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: "SETTLES"
    │
    ▼
  CouponKeyService.firstUnique()
    │ pass 1 (LinkedHashMap, insertion order):
    │   S:2  E:2  T:2  L:1
    │ pass 2 (iterate in order):
    │   S(2) skip → E(2) skip → T(2) skip → L(1)
    ▼
  return 'L'

  "AABB" → A:2 B:2 → no count==1 → return null (NONE)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the first non-repeating character means finding the earliest character in the string that appears exactly once. I solve it with two passes over a LinkedHashMap. In the first pass I count the frequency of every character, and in the second pass I iterate the map and return the first character whose count is one. The whole thing is linear time, and the space is proportional to the number of distinct characters, which is bounded by the alphabet.

The reason I specifically choose a LinkedHashMap rather than a plain HashMap is ordering. A plain HashMap does not remember the order in which I inserted the keys, so I could not reliably determine which unique character came first. A LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, so when I iterate it the characters come out in the order they first appeared in the string, which is exactly what the word first means in this problem.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to derive a sub-key for promotional coupon codes. From a generated code I pick the first letter that appears only once, which reduces collisions in a secondary index. I also handle the case where no character is unique, such as a code where every letter repeats, by returning a clear sentinel instead of crashing, so the calling code can fall back to another key-generation strategy gracefully.
